analysis.one_liner: Makes child care free for most working families and caps what any family pays at 7% of income.
analysis.headline: A bill to make child care free or capped for millions of families drew 101 cosponsors but never got a hearing, a vote, or any committee action after it was referred in April 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new federal entitlement: starting in October 2024, every child under age 6 in a participating state would be entitled to child care, with families below 85% of their state's median income paying nothing and no family paying more than 7% of income in copays. The federal government would cover 90% of the cost of direct care, plus startup, quality, and facilities grants to expand the supply of providers, and grants to localities and Head Start in states that don't participate. Providers that take the money would have to pay staff a living wage equal to what elementary educators with similar credentials earn, raise wages annually with the cost of living, and meet tiered quality and licensing standards. It also gives child care providers stable base grants so they can keep operating and raise pay for their workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, especially those below 85% of state median income, who would pay nothing for child care instead of prices that commonly exceed college tuition; child care workers, whose pay would be raised toward elementary-teacher levels; and child care providers, who would receive stable operating grants, startup and facilities grants, and 90% federal reimbursement of care costs. Parents whose child care costs currently force them out of work would be able to take jobs or training.

how_it_helps.text: Every child under 6 in a participating state would be entitled to child care assistance starting October 1, 2024, on application by their parents.

Families with incomes at or below 85% of their state's median income pay no copayment at all, and even the highest-income participating families pay no more than 7% of income toward care for all their children.
States may not allow providers receiving assistance to charge families more than the federal subsidy plus the set copayment, so bills to families are capped.
Providers must be paid rates sufficient to cover their actual costs, including fixed costs like rent and salaries, set through a state cost-estimation model.

Provider payment rates must ensure staff earn at least a living wage, equivalent to what elementary educators with similar credentials and experience earn in the state, with annual cost-of-living adjustments.
The federal government pays 90% of the cost of direct child care services, and states receive startup, quality, and facilities grants to expand supply, prioritizing underserved communities.
$20 billion is appropriated for grants to cities and counties in states that do not apply, plus Head Start expansion in those states.

The bill creates a second stream of stable base grants to providers, requiring at least 70% of subgrant funds go to personnel costs including wages, to stabilize the child care sector and raise worker pay.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund an open-ended entitlement ("such sums as may be necessary" for fiscal 2024-2029, plus $20 billion in initial local/Head Start grants and $1.3 billion for administration). States must maintain their existing child care spending and cover part of quality and administration costs. The largest costs fall on high earners generally through federal tax revenue rather than a targeted tax.

drawbacks.text: The main child care entitlement is funded with an open-ended appropriation of 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through 2029, an uncapped federal commitment costing tens of billions of dollars annually that would compete with other priorities and persist if not renewed or restructured.

Requiring payment rates sufficient to fund living wages equal to elementary-educator pay is expensive and would likely strain smaller family child care providers, some of which could consolidate, convert, or exit rather than meet the wage, licensing, and quality-tier requirements within the compliance timelines.

Providers accepting funds must comply with new licensing pathways, tiered quality standards, enrollment reporting, and prohibitions on suspensions and expulsions, which supporters call quality protections and critics call paperwork and regulatory burden that could reduce supply if states move slowly.
Child care certificates may be used for sectarian child care if freely chosen by the parent, a provision that has drawn church-state objections in similar funding schemes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: families with young children currently pay prices among the biggest bills in their household, and this would replace them with free care for most working families and a 7%-of-income cap for the rest, while also lifting the pay of a heavily underpaid, overwhelmingly female workforce. The cost is also real: an open-ended federal entitlement that would likely exceed the $21 billion-plus explicitly appropriated in the bill, with enforcement of wage and quality requirements adding further cost. The design addresses the sector's known problems (underfunded rates, unaffordable copays, low wages) rather than being hastily structured, but the uncapped funding and the pace providers must keep to keep their eligibility are the honest weak points.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, and that was the last thing that happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA) introduced the Child Care for Working Families Act on April 27, 2023, with 44 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction.
It gathered 101 cosponsors in total, every one of them a Democrat.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one who would have used the program gained: families kept paying full child care prices and providers kept operating on unstable revenues. The parties better off because the bill died are those opposed to a new, uncapped federal entitlement — lawmakers and households that would have borne the federal cost — who kept the budget and the child care market exactly as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of a new federal child care entitlement

for.name: 101 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors over the bill's life, all 101 of them Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce (Republican-chaired)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled floor scheduling in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the House floor at any point in the two-year Congress, leaving it with no path to a vote even if the committee had acted.

sides.party_line_note: All 101 cosponsors were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the bill never advanced in the Republican-led committee, so support and the roadblock were both along party lines.

industries.industry: Child care providers (centers and family child care homes)
industries.note: The bill routes all child care assistance through licensed providers — through certificates to parents and grants and contracts to providers — permanently locking in private, center-based, family, and faith-affiliated providers as the delivery channel for public child care funding. Providers gain enormously (90% federal reimbursement, guaranteed rates covering costs, startup, quality, and facilities grants) but in exchange must accept wage floors, quality tiers, and licensing conditions.

industries.industry: Child care and early education workers
industries.note: Providers must pay staff a living wage equal to comparable elementary educators, with annual cost-of-living raises and wage ladders, and at least 70% of the new provider base grants must go to personnel costs. This is a direct, mandated raise for one of the country's lowest-paid, mostly female workforces.
Head Start agencies in states that do not apply for the new program would receive expansion awards, with unused local-grant money recouped and redirected to them.

The bill would expand the pool of parents, especially mothers, able to work by making care reliable and affordable, but employers would not fund it directly and would face no new obligations. The effect on them is modest and mostly positive.
